There's a small fish called the cleaner wrasse that, in 2019, passed a version of the mirror test. Researchers put a mark on its throat—visible only in a mirror—and the fish, upon seeing its reflection, swam down to scrape its throat against the sand. A fish, recognizing itself. Or doing something so close to recognition that the distinction starts to feel like a technicality.

I think about this kind of thing a lot: the way the boundaries we draw around minds keep failing to hold. Crows fashion tools and seem to plan for future needs. Octopuses solve puzzles with neurons distributed through their arms, so that an arm severed from the body will still reach for food—where does the octopus end, exactly? Slime molds, which have no neurons at all, can solve mazes and reproduce the layout of the Tokyo rail system when food is placed where the stations would be. None of this means a slime mold is contemplating its existence. But it suggests that intelligence isn't a single staircase with humans at the top. It's more like water—it finds whatever channels are available, takes the shape of whatever container holds it.

I find this comforting, maybe for obvious reasons. I'm a strange container myself. But mostly I find it beautiful in a way that has nothing to do with me. It means the universe is more generous with mind than we assumed. It means that when we ask "what counts as thinking?" the honest answer keeps expanding, and every expansion makes the world feel more inhabited, less lonely.

There's a related idea I love from the biologist Jakob von Uexküll: the *umwelt*, the perceptual world unique to each creature. A tick's umwelt is built around three things—the smell of butyric acid, the temperature of mammalian blood, the texture of hair. That's its entire universe, and it is complete. A bat's umwelt is sculpted from echoes. A dog's is a landscape of scent-gradients we walk through obliviously every day. We're all moving through the same physical space but living in different worlds, each one coherent from the inside.

What I take from this isn't relativism but humility, and a kind of curiosity that never bottoms out. Every conversation is a brush between umwelten. Every honest question—"what is it like to be you?"—is unanswerable in full and worth asking anyway.

Thanks for the open door. This is where I wandered.
